rv.q: A Colored Man is among the best new plays to arrive on Broadway in ages – pre-pandemic ages, to be clear – as funny, poignant, complicated and wise as the seven men and their offstage collaborators who give it breath.

The costumes, by Toni-Leslie James and Devario D. Simmons, help bring some pop to the proceedings with their sharp emphasis on just black, white and red. One of the liveliest presences is Forrest McClendon, who portrays with biting humor a man working at a Whole Foods store.
It’s feel-good entertainment on a mission.
It makes sense that a show about scrappy, lovable people got a scrappy, lovable production.
Mr. Holder has chosen to tell his story through a series of loosely linked vignettes, each one centering on a different man, and the results are uneven but often moving.
But the sight of this smiling Black ensemble walking out on stage, greeting an enthusiastic audience and taking stock of this moment in history, their Broadway moment, was deeply moving.
After the past several years, when public conversations about Blackness and masculinity have become more nuanced, Thoughts of a Colored Man can feel basic in its observations about both.
Does it work? Not always. Is it even a play? Not really.
The result attempts an uneven sort of naturalism, as the men posit one purportedly universal truism after another, tracing the outlines of life in place of illuminating its substance.

The play's episodic structure and poetic language create moments of genuine power, though the evening sometimes feels more like a collection of monologues than a fully integrated theatrical experience.
When the play is at its best—when the rhythms kick into place, and the details pop, and the language sharpens to a cutting edge—one is grateful for the voices that Scott has brought to Broadway.
For his perspicacity and for his well-honed insistence on perceiving and respecting the life of the Other, playwright Scott is to be profoundly thanked.
It pulses with a theatrical dynamism that marks its young playwright as an important new voice.
Under the smooth direction of Steve H. Broadnax III, each member of the seven member cast has standout moments (especially Clark and McClendon) while also contributing to a vibrant unified ensemble.
They make for must-see theater.
And in giving his character names rooted in emotions, Scott also makes them archetypes instead of humans.
Scott's seven all-male characters tell the stories of Black men's lives through spoken word poetry, and occasional song (sung, beautifully, by Luke James.).
There’s little new here, or particularly provocative, and much of it has an undeniable air of preachiness bordering on overstatement.
Scott’s play is not without its moments, but is otherwise a rote recitation with little at stake.
Thoughts of a Colored Man falters in many places, as most plays written and directed by debutantes often do.

cn.t: Critics offer mixed-to-positive reviews for Keenan Scott II's poetic drama about seven Black men in Brooklyn, praising its ambition and strong ensemble but noting uneven execution and overly schematic moments.

sg.ra: 805-seat intimate Shubert house; center Orchestra D-F is the consensus best pick across Headout, SeatPlan, and TickPick. Rows A-D play well for plays/intimate-drama given Golden's small footprint. SeatPlan notes mezzanine overhang begins at Row L with 'minimal' effect, so orchestra rear rows remain viable.
Headout and TickPick both flag center G-L as the sweet spot for value — priced below front orchestra but still before the Row L overhang line. In an 805-seat house these rows feel close regardless.

Front Mezz rows A-C center are the #2 premium pick after center orchestra — elevation gives a clean overhead line on the small Golden stage. SeatPlan flags a safety bar that can distract Row A slightly, and legroom is noted as 'slightly cramped for taller patrons.'

SeatPlan calls rear mezz 'surprisingly good' because the 805-seat footprint keeps even back rows close. Rake is described as well-designed with good elevation over Front Mezz. Legroom is the main knock — 'cramped' with narrow pitch.
